Appendix A Additional Results

For spin-0 mediators, we previously chose benchmarks where we fixed the dark matter - mediator mass ratio: ma,ϕ=3​mχ​v0m_{a,\phi}=3m_{\chi}v_{0} for a heavy mediator and ma,ϕ=0.3​mχ​v0m_{a,\phi}=0.3m_{\chi}v_{0} for a light mediator. This somewhat arbitrary condition can be relaxed, such that a heavy (light) mediator would correspond to any ma,ϕ≥3​ma,χ​v0m_{a,\phi}\geq 3m_{a,\chi}v_{0} (mϕ≤0.3​mχ​v0m_{\phi}\leq 0.3m_{\chi}v_{0}). One can then open up the most parameter space by marginalizing over all possible mediator masses for each point in mχm_{\chi} and choosing the mediator mass that produces the weakest existing constraint on the reference cross section.

In Figs. 9 and 10, these optimized bounds are shown in comparison to our default heavy benchmark bounds. The light benchmark ma,ϕ=0.3​mχ​v0m_{a,\phi}=0.3m_{\chi}v_{0} presented in Section VI.1 already optimizes the parameter space, and we therefore do not show new plots for the light mediator case. The new exclusion curves are denoted by dashed grey and blue lines, corresponding to the bounds assuming the SN trapping window is open or closed, respectively. The left panels of Figs. 9 and 10 assume fD​M=1f_{DM}=1 and therefore the optimization process considers both the SIDM constraint on gχg_{\chi} as well as the various experimental constraints on gpg_{p}. On the right, we assume a small fraction of DM (fD​M=0.05)(f_{DM}=0.05) which relaxes the SIDM constraints. For these plots, we set gχ=1g_{\chi}=1 and optimize over the experimental constraints on gpg_{p}.

For the heavy mediator, when the SN trapping window is open, a new wedge of parameter space is opened for mχ≲100m_{\chi}\lesssim 100 MeV by fixing the mediator mass at about 0.3 MeV, above the horizontal branch constraints and inside the trapping window. In the case where the SN trapping window is closed and fD​M=1f_{DM}=1, additional parameter space is opened by allowing for heavier mediator masses which allows for a substantially larger gpg_{p} and gχg_{\chi}. In this case, the cross section bound is weakened by considering ma,ϕ∼100m_{a,\phi}\sim 100 MeV and below the accelerator bounds.

The separation here into heavy and light mediators, with somewhat arbitrary cutoffs, may leave one wondering whether there is open parameter space in the intermediate range of mediator masses 0.3​mχ​v0<mϕ,a<3​mχ​v00.3m_{\chi}v_{0}<m_{\phi,a}<3m_{\chi}v_{0}. We verified that the amount of open parameter space does not shift significantly based on this choice.

While the above optimization appears to open up more parameter space for MeV-scale dark matter, the mass scales and couplings here could face additional constraints from cosmology. In fact, for these couplings, χ\chi scattering leads to χ\chi thermalization, likely resulting in tension with the NeffN_{\rm eff} measurement from BBN. To avoid χ\chi thermalization, the scattering rate of χ​χ→{a,ϕ}​{a,ϕ}\chi\chi\rightarrow\{a,\phi\}\{a,\phi\} must be less than the Hubble scale when neutrinos decouple, forcing gχg_{\chi} to be very small. Again, in this scenario, all parameter space opened by the optimization is ruled out. Alternatively, one may assume a very low reheating scale, such that the DM was never in thermal equilibrium. This case is the most optimistic and allows gpg_{p} to live in the trapping window, opening up significant parameter space. However, attaining the correct DM relic density with such a low reheating scale is a nontrivial task and should not be assumed lightly.

In conclusion, while carefully selecting the mediator mass can open up some potential parameter space, it is important to consider the cosmological implications of such a choice. Much of the parameter space in the new wedge likely requires non-trivial model building to avoid tension with the NeffN_{\rm eff} measurement from BBN.

Appendix B Caveats related to CHARM bound

We note several caveats in interpreting recent recasts of the CHARM experiment bound on the ALP parameter space [41, 89, 90]. First, the CHARM collaboration used two estimators for the reconstruction and selection of events from axion decays inside the detector volume [40]. The first estimator is a measure of the deviation of the shower axis from the beam direction and the second estimator is a measure of the transverse width of the shower, both of which are highly sensitive to the boost of the axion, leading to a fiducial efficiency that depends on the axion mass. These estimators have only been mentioned briefly in the CHARM paper [40], such that modeling them reliably at this point in time may not be possible. In all reinterpretations that we know of, a constant fiducial efficiency has been applied, and the mass dependence of the efficiency has not been taken into account in the literature. It is not clear how valid this approximation is.

Second, fermion contributions (generated by RGE running) to the kaon decay width into an axion generally have been neglected. We find that the RG-generated off-diagonal down-strange-ALP coupling dominates the contribution from the cG​Gc_{GG} coupling in the amplitude of KL→π0​aK_{L}\to\pi^{0}a, by at least an order of magnitude. This may lead to an O⁡(1)O(1) correction to the constraints quoted in the literature.

Appendix C Axial vector model UV completion

As a proof-of-concept, we construct a UV-complete model of an axial vector with couplings to SM baryons and suppressed couplings to the charged leptons, as in (38). In this model, the coupling of the dark matter to the A′A^{\prime} is predicted to be half that of the SM quarks to the A′A^{\prime}. In Appendix D, we will attempt to construct a more involved model in which this prediction can be relaxed.

The model is based on a new U​(1)′U(1)^{\prime} gauge symmetry; the full matter content is shown in Table 3. We assume for simplicity that the A′A^{\prime} couples universally to all three quark generations, and assume Dirac neutrinos with sterile components NN. The NN field is also charged with respect to A′A^{\prime}.

We must include a set of heavy fermions (see e.g. [91]) to cancel the gauge anomalies, a scalar field ϕ\phi which breaks the U​(1)′U(1)^{\prime} spontaneously, and two new Higgs inert doublets Hu′H_{u}^{\prime} and Hd′H_{d}^{\prime}, which are responsible for generating the SM Yukawa interactions. These are given in the second block of Table 3. The heavy fermions are vector-like relative to the SM gauge groups, and as such the SM gauge anomalies continue to cancel trivially. The theory is now also vector-like relative to the U​(1)′U(1)^{\prime} charges, meaning that the only non-trivial anomalies are the mixed U​(1)′U(1)^{\prime}-SM anomalies, which cancel as well. The mass terms for the anomalon fields are generated by the interactions

ℒ⊃\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\supset λQ​ϕ​Q′​Q¯′+λu​ϕ†​u′​u¯′+λd​ϕ†​d′​d¯′+ϕ2ΛN​N′​N¯′.\displaystyle\lambda_{Q}\phi Q^{\prime}\bar{Q}^{\prime}+\lambda_{u}\phi^{\dagger}u^{\prime}\bar{u}^{\prime}+\lambda_{d}\phi^{\dagger}d^{\prime}\bar{d}^{\prime}+\frac{\phi^{2}}{\Lambda_{N}}N^{\prime}\bar{N}^{\prime}. (85)

The last term in (85) has operator dimension 5, but can be UV completed easily. The N′N^{\prime} and N¯′\bar{N}^{\prime} also play no role in the phenomenology, other than anomaly cancellation. They can therefore be significantly lighter than the remaining fermions in (85) without running into existing bounds of any sort.

The LHC bounds on the colored fermions Q′,Q¯′Q^{\prime},\bar{Q}^{\prime}, etc., depend on their assumed decay and production channels, as reviewed in [57]. If we consider only hadronic decays, the current bounds on a single generation vector-like fermion range between 800 GeV and 1400 GeV [92], depending on the assummed branching ratios and representation under the SM gauge group. We therefore require that their masses ≳1\gtrsim 1 TeV for all twelve vector-like quarks, which we consider to be conservative. We further assume λQ,u,d≲1\lambda_{Q,u,d}\lesssim 1, to avoid excessive fine-tuning and Landau poles at a low energy scale. This is because the field ϕ\phi couples to all twelve Dirac fermions in (85) which carry three colors each. This leads to a large correction to ϕ\phi’s potential, even for λQ,u,d≈1\lambda_{Q,u,d}\approx 1 and a very low UV cutoff scale. With these assumptions, we find that we need to impose ⟨ϕ⟩≳1\langle\phi\rangle\gtrsim 1 TeV in (85) to satisfy the LHC bounds on the anomalon fields. The field ϕ\phi also generates the mass of the A′A^{\prime}, such that we can obtain the bound

g′≲12​mA′TeV.g^{\prime}\lesssim\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\frac{m_{A^{\prime}}}{\mathrm{TeV}}. (86)

We note that σ¯A′∼g′4\bar{\sigma}_{A^{\prime}}\sim g^{\prime 4}, which means that the bound shown in Fig. 8 is rather sensitive to the assumptions we make about the UV theory. The bound on σ¯A′\bar{\sigma}_{A^{\prime}} could therefore easily be weaker by an order of magnitude or more if one assumes more aggressive values for either λQ,u,d\lambda_{Q,u,d} or if the LHC bounds can be relaxed, e.g. by assuming a final state with a large number of soft jets. Still, this would not affect the conclusions we have drawn in Section VI.2.

Next, we must generate the Yukawa couplings for quarks and leptons with the SM Higgs, HH. This can be achieved using the Hu,d′H_{u,d}^{\prime} interactions [93]

ℒ⊃\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\supset yeHLe+YU(Hu′)c†Qu+YDHd′Qd+YE(Hu′)c†LN\displaystyle\,y_{e}HLe+Y_{U}(H_{u}^{\prime})^{c\dagger}Qu+Y_{D}H_{d}^{\prime}Qd+Y_{E}(H_{u}^{\prime})^{c\dagger}LN
+λ~u​ϕ2​Hu′​H+λ~d​ϕ2​Hd′​H†−mHu′2​|Hu′|2−mHd′2​|Hd′|2\displaystyle+\tilde{\lambda}_{u}\phi^{2}H_{u}^{\prime}H+\tilde{\lambda}_{d}\phi^{2}H_{d}^{\prime}H^{\dagger}-m^{2}_{H^{\prime}_{u}}|H^{\prime}_{u}|^{2}-m^{2}_{H^{\prime}_{d}}|H^{\prime}_{d}|^{2}
+h.c.\displaystyle+\rm{h.c.} (87)

where Hu,dc≡i​σ2​Hu,d∗H_{u,d}^{c}\equiv i\sigma_{2}H_{u,d}^{*}. Upon integrating out the heavy fields Hu,d′H_{u,d}^{\prime}, and spontaneously breaking the U​(1)′U(1)^{\prime} by allowing ϕ\phi to pick up a vev77 7 For simplicity, we consider the case where ⟨Hu,d′⟩=0\langle H_{u,d}^{\prime}\rangle=0., these terms in the Lagrangian lead to the Yukawa interactions

ℒ⊃yu​Q​(Hc)​u+yd​Q​H​d+yN​L​(Hc)​N+h.c.\mathcal{L}\supset y_{u}Q(H^{c})u+y_{d}QHd+y_{N}L(H^{c})N+\rm{h.c.} (88)

where

yu,d∼YU,D​λ~u,d​⟨ϕ⟩2mHu,d′2,yN∼YE​λ~u​⟨ϕ⟩2mHu′2.y_{u,d}\sim Y_{U,D}\tilde{\lambda}_{u,d}\frac{\langle\phi\rangle^{2}}{m^{2}_{H_{u,d}^{\prime}}},~~~y_{N}\sim Y_{E}\tilde{\lambda}_{u}\frac{\langle\phi\rangle^{2}}{m^{2}_{H_{u}^{\prime}}}. (89)

For the dark sector, we use the UV completion put forward in [65]. In particular, to cancel the gauge anomalies we need a pair of Weyl fermions χ1,2\chi_{1,2} with charge −1/2-1/2 and along with a pair χ¯1,2\bar{\chi}_{1,2} with charge 1/21/2, given in the third block of Table 3. The dark sector Yukawa interactions are

yχ​ϕ​χ1​χ2+y¯χ​ϕ†​χ¯1​χ¯2+h.c.\displaystyle y_{\chi}\phi\chi_{1}\chi_{2}+\bar{y}_{\chi}\phi^{\dagger}\bar{\chi}_{1}\bar{\chi}_{2}~+\rm{h.c.} (90)

The vectorlike mass terms of the form χ1,2​χ¯1,2\chi_{1,2}\bar{\chi}_{1,2} are assumed to be absent or heavily suppressed. This is needed to suppress the coupling of the A′A^{\prime} to the dark matter vector-current. We identify the Dirac fermion composed out of the Weyl fermions χ≡(χ1,χ2†)\chi\equiv(\chi_{1},\chi_{2}^{\dagger}) with the dark matter. We further assume that y¯χ>yχ\bar{y}_{\chi}>y_{\chi}, such that the Dirac fermion associated with χ¯1\bar{\chi}_{1} and χ¯2\bar{\chi}_{2} is always heavier than χ\chi. Going forward, we will assume that the annihilation rate of this heavier fermion to either χ\chi or A′A^{\prime} is efficient enough that we can neglect its residual relic density. The mass parameters of the dark sector particles are given by

mA′2\displaystyle m_{A^{\prime}}^{2} =2​g′2​⟨ϕ⟩2\displaystyle=2g^{\prime 2}\langle\phi\rangle^{2} (91)
mϕ2\displaystyle m_{\phi}^{2} =2​λ​⟨ϕ⟩2\displaystyle=2\lambda\langle\phi\rangle^{2} (92)
mχ\displaystyle m_{\chi} =yχ​⟨ϕ⟩,\displaystyle=y_{\chi}\langle\phi\rangle, (93)

with mϕm_{\phi} the mass of the physical scalar and with λ\lambda the quartic coupling of the potential of ϕ\phi, normalized as λ2​|ϕ|4\frac{\lambda}{2}|\phi|^{4}. Analogous to (86), we find the following constraint on g′g^{\prime}

g′=yχ2​mA′mχ≲12​mA′mχ,g^{\prime}=\frac{y_{\chi}}{\sqrt{2}}\frac{m_{A^{\prime}}}{m_{\chi}}\lesssim\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\frac{m_{A^{\prime}}}{m_{\chi}}, (94)

where in the last step, we have taken yχ≲1y_{\chi}\lesssim 1 to avoid the non-perturbative regime. In practice, this bound will always be weaker than the bound in (86) for the parameter space of interest.

In conclusion, we constructed a UV completion for the axial A′A^{\prime} mediator, though it requires a fair amount of additional fields in the ultraviolet to ensure all anomalies are canceled. These extra colored particles must be beyond the current LHC limits, which limits the size of g′g^{\prime} in the infrared. Moreover, the model predicts the relation (38), resulting in

gχ∼gn∼gp,g_{\chi}\sim g_{n}\sim g_{p}, (95)

which is undesirable for direct detection. In the next appendix, we attempt to construct a non-minimal model which is not subject to the parametric constraint in (95).

Appendix D A generalized axial vector model?

As shown in Section VI.2, there are no realistic direct detection prospects for sub-GeV dark matter if the dark matter-mediator coupling gχg_{\chi} is tied to the mediator-SM coupling gpg_{p} for the axial A′A^{\prime} model. It is therefore worthwhile to investigate whether this constraint can be relaxed, such that gχg_{\chi} is much larger. In other words, can we construct a model for which one can take gχ≫gp,ng_{\chi}\gg g_{p,n} in (3)? In this appendix, we argue that it is challenging to write such a model, and one should therefore be wary of assuming gp,n≪gχg_{p,n}\ll g_{\chi} without a detailed UV justification.

D.1 A second gauge field is needed

First, one may simply attempt to assign a large charge |Qχ||Q_{\chi}| to χ1,2\chi_{1,2}, such that gχ≡|Qχ|​g′≫g′∼gp,ng_{\chi}\equiv|Q_{\chi}|g^{\prime}\gg g^{\prime}\sim g_{p,n}. In Appendix C, we assigned charges Qχ=−1/2Q_{\chi}=-1/2 so that a single scalar field ϕ\phi could generate both the Yukawa terms for SM fields as well as the dark sector masses. There, the charge of the scalar field was fixed by the need to provide mass terms for the anomalon fields in (85). By assigning a large QχQ_{\chi}, we require an additional scalar field to ensure that the mass terms in (90) remain allowed by gauge invariance. Concretely, we now need two fields ϕ1\phi_{1} and ϕ2\phi_{2} with couplings

ℒ⊃λQ​ϕ1​Q′​Q¯′+⋯+yχ​ϕ2​χ1​χ2,\mathcal{L}\supset\lambda_{Q}\phi_{1}Q^{\prime}\bar{Q}^{\prime}+\cdots+y_{\chi}\phi_{2}\chi_{1}\chi_{2}, (96)

where ϕ1\phi_{1} and ϕ2\phi_{2} have charge +1+1 and −2​Qχ-2Q_{\chi}, respectively, under the U​(1)′U(1)^{\prime} gauge symmetry. The model now has two accidental global symmetries which are broken spontaneously by ⟨ϕ1⟩\langle\phi_{1}\rangle and ⟨ϕ2⟩\langle\phi_{2}\rangle:

ϕ1→e−2​i​αϕ1,Q′→ei​αQ′,Q¯′→ei​αQ¯′,etc.\displaystyle\phi_{1}\to e^{-2i\alpha}\phi_{1},\;\;Q^{\prime}\to e^{i\alpha}Q^{\prime},\;\;\bar{Q}^{\prime}\to e^{i\alpha}\bar{Q}^{\prime},\;\;\text{etc.}
ϕ2→e−2​i​βϕ2,χ1→ei​βχ1,χ2→ei​βχ2,etc.\displaystyle\phi_{2}\to e^{-2i\beta}\phi_{2},\;\;\chi_{1}\to e^{i\beta}\chi_{1},\;\;\chi_{2}\to e^{i\beta}\chi_{2},\;\;\text{etc.} (97)

One linear combination of the corresponding Goldstone bosons is eaten by the Aμ′A^{\prime}_{\mu}, while the other one is exactly massless. At one loop, this particle moreover picks up a coupling to photons through the first term in (96). To avoid violating astrophysical bounds on massless particles with a coupling to photons, one would need to assume that the overlap between the uneaten Goldstone mode and ϕ1\phi_{1} is extremely tiny. This would correspond to assuming ⟨ϕ1⟩≫Qχ​⟨ϕ2⟩\langle\phi_{1}\rangle\gg Q_{\chi}\langle\phi_{2}\rangle, which is incompatible with our earlier Qχ≫1Q_{\chi}\gg 1 assumption.

Alternatively, the mass of the Goldstone can be lifted by breaking the symmetries in (97) explicitly down to the linear combination corresponding the U​(1)′U(1)^{\prime} gauge symmetry. The lowest dimensional operator that achieves this while respecting gauge invariance is

ℒ⊃1Λ2​Qχ−2​ϕ12​Qχ​ϕ2+h.c.\mathcal{L}\supset\frac{1}{\Lambda^{2Q_{\chi}-2}}\phi_{1}^{2Q_{\chi}}\phi_{2}+\text{h.c.} (98)

This operator is extremely irrelevant for Qχ≫1Q_{\chi}\gg 1 and is therefore not an effective way to lift the mass of the Goldstone.

A straightforward solution is to gauge the second accidental U​(1)′U(1)^{\prime} symmetry as well, such that the Goldstone mode is eaten. This means that the visible and dark sectors each have their own axial U​(1)′U(1)^{\prime} gauge symmetry, whose gauge couplings need not be related to each other. The interaction between the visible and dark sectors can then be engineered by mixing the two A′A^{\prime} fields. The matter content of this theory is shown in Table 4. As alluded to before, each U​(1)′U(1)^{\prime} must be broken by its own scalar field ϕ1,2\phi_{1,2}, which is also responsible for generating the mass terms of all the fermions in their sector, fully analogous to the discussion in Appendix C.

D.2 Heavy mediator limit

Our primary interest is to investigate whether we can construct a model that is not subject to the gp∼gχg_{p}\sim g_{\chi} constraint and reduces to the Hamiltonian (8). We therefore consider the heavy mediator limit, where mA1,mA2≫qm_{A_{1}},m_{A_{2}}\gg q.

First, one may consider mixing A1′A_{1}^{\prime} and A2′A_{2}^{\prime} through a kinetic mixing operator

ℒ⊃ϵ2​F1′μ​ν​F2,μ​ν′.\mathcal{L}\supset\frac{\epsilon}{2}F_{1}^{\prime\mu\nu}F_{2,\mu\nu}^{\prime}. (99)

Because of the derivative couplings in this operator, its effects vanish in the q→0q\to 0 limit. It therefore does not reproduce (8).

The mixing between the gauge fields must therefore occur through the mass matrix of the A′A^{\prime} fields, rather than their kinetic terms. To achieve this, we must add a third scalar, φ\varphi, which is charged under both fields. Its vacuum expectation value will mix the A1′A_{1}^{\prime} and A2′A_{2}^{\prime}, thus enabling the SM - dark sector interaction that is needed for direct detection.88 8 This additional scalar once again introduces an unwanted Goldstone boson, however in this instance it can be lifted easily by adding the relevant operator ϕ1​φ​ϕ2\phi_{1}\varphi\phi_{2} to the Lagrangian. Concretely, the mass matrix for the gauge bosons is

mA2=(m12δ​m2δ​m2m22),m_{A}^{2}=\left(\!\begin{array}[]{cc}m_{1}^{2}&\delta m^{2}\\ \delta m^{2}&m_{2}^{2}\end{array}\!\right), (100)

with

m12=\displaystyle m_{1}^{2}= 2​g12​(|⟨ϕ1⟩|2+|⟨φ⟩|2)\displaystyle 2g_{1}^{2}(|\langle\phi_{1}\rangle|^{2}+|\langle\varphi\rangle|^{2})
m22=\displaystyle m_{2}^{2}= 2​g22​(|⟨ϕ2⟩|2+|⟨φ⟩|2)\displaystyle 2g_{2}^{2}(|\langle\phi_{2}\rangle|^{2}+|\langle\varphi\rangle|^{2})
δ​m2=\displaystyle\delta m^{2}= 2​g1​g2​|⟨φ⟩|2,\displaystyle 2g_{1}g_{2}|\langle\varphi\rangle|^{2}, (101)

Since we will assume g1≪g2∼1g_{1}\ll g_{2}\sim 1, it follows that δ​m≪m2\delta m\ll m_{2} regardless of relative size of the three vacuum expectation values.

First, let us consider the case with m1<m2m_{1}<m_{2}. Denoting the lightest and heaviest mass eigenstates with AℓμA^{\mu}_{\ell} and AhμA^{\mu}_{h}, respectively, we find

mAℓ2\displaystyle m^{2}_{A_{\ell}} ≈m12−δ​m4m22−m12\displaystyle\approx m_{1}^{2}-\frac{\delta m^{4}}{m_{2}^{2}-m_{1}^{2}} (102)
mAh2\displaystyle m^{2}_{A_{h}} ≈m22+δ​m4m22−m12,\displaystyle\approx m_{2}^{2}+\frac{\delta m^{4}}{m_{2}^{2}-m_{1}^{2}}, (103)

where we expanded in δ​m2≪m22−m12\delta m^{2}\ll m_{2}^{2}-m_{1}^{2}. The mass eigenstates couple to the visible and dark sector currents through

ℒ⊃\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\supset Aℓμ​(g1​J1,μ−g2​δ​m2m22−m12​J2,μ)\displaystyle A_{\ell}^{\mu}\left(g_{1}J_{1,\mu}-g_{2}\frac{\delta m^{2}}{m_{2}^{2}-m_{1}^{2}}J_{2,\mu}\right) (104)
+Ahμ​(g2​J2,μ+g1​δ​m2m22−m12​J1,μ),\displaystyle+A_{h}^{\mu}\left(g_{2}J_{2,\mu}+g_{1}\frac{\delta m^{2}}{m_{2}^{2}-m_{1}^{2}}J_{1,\mu}\right), (105)

where J1,μJ_{1,\mu} and J2,μJ_{2,\mu} are the SM and dark matter axial currents

J1μ\displaystyle J_{1}^{\mu} ≡q¯​γμ​γ5​q\displaystyle\equiv\bar{q}\gamma^{\mu}\gamma_{5}q (106)
J2μ\displaystyle J_{2}^{\mu} ≡−12​χ¯​γμ​γ5​χ.\displaystyle\equiv-\frac{1}{2}\bar{\chi}\gamma^{\mu}\gamma_{5}\chi. (107)

The leading contribution to the direct detection scattering rate will be through the exchange of the AℓA_{\ell}. The Hamiltonian for direct detection is that in (8) with

gn,p\displaystyle g_{n,p} ∼g1\displaystyle\sim g_{1} (108)
gχ\displaystyle g_{\chi} =12​δ​m2m22−m12​g2\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\frac{\delta m^{2}}{m_{2}^{2}-m_{1}^{2}}g_{2} (109)
mA′\displaystyle m_{A^{\prime}} =mAℓ,\displaystyle=m_{A_{\ell}}, (110)

where we have used the ∼\sim since e.g., the neutron/proton coupling will also contain a form factor (see 40). Plugging in (101), we find that

|gχ|≤|gp,n|2,|g_{\chi}|\leq\frac{|g_{p,n}|}{2}, (111)

which is incompatible with the |gχ|≫|gp,n||g_{\chi}|\gg|g_{p,n}| hierarchy we seek.

Alternatively, we could have chosen m1>m2m_{1}>m_{2} by taking ⟨ϕ1⟩≫⟨ϕ2⟩,⟨φ⟩\langle\phi_{1}\rangle\gg\langle\phi_{2}\rangle,\langle\varphi\rangle. The AℓA_{\ell} now predominantly aligns with the dark sector U​(1)′U(1)^{\prime} (A2μA_{2}^{\mu}) and we find

mAℓ2\displaystyle m^{2}_{A_{\ell}} ≈m22−δ​m4m12−m22\displaystyle\approx m_{2}^{2}-\frac{\delta m^{4}}{m_{1}^{2}-m_{2}^{2}} (112)
mAh2\displaystyle m^{2}_{A_{h}} ≈m12+δ​m4m12−m22,\displaystyle\approx m_{1}^{2}+\frac{\delta m^{4}}{m_{1}^{2}-m_{2}^{2}}, (113)

and

ℒ⊃\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\supset Aℓμ​(−g2​J2,μ+g1​δ​m2m12−m22​J1,μ)\displaystyle A_{\ell}^{\mu}\left(-g_{2}J_{2,\mu}+g_{1}\frac{\delta m^{2}}{m_{1}^{2}-m_{2}^{2}}J_{1,\mu}\right) (114)
+Ahμ​(g1​J1,μ+g2​δ​m2m12−m22​J2,μ).\displaystyle+A_{h}^{\mu}\left(g_{1}J_{1,\mu}+g_{2}\frac{\delta m^{2}}{m_{1}^{2}-m_{2}^{2}}J_{2,\mu}\right). (115)

To avoid suppressing the mixing angle further, we need to take m1∼m2m_{1}\sim m_{2}, since we already have the hierarchy δ​m≪m2\delta m\ll m_{2} from (101). There is therefore only a small hierarchy between the mass eigenstates (mAℓ≲mAhm_{A_{\ell}}\lesssim m_{A_{h}}). All the bounds in Section IV moreover apply to the AhA_{h}, such that we must still impose g1≪1g_{1}\ll 1.

Again plugging in (101), we now find that the couplings of the AℓA_{\ell} can be identified with (8) through

gn,p\displaystyle g_{n,p} ∼δ​m2m12−m22​g1≲g12g2\displaystyle\sim\frac{\delta m^{2}}{m_{1}^{2}-m_{2}^{2}}g_{1}\lesssim\frac{g_{1}^{2}}{g_{2}} (116)
gχ\displaystyle g_{\chi} =g2.\displaystyle=g_{2}. (117)

This realizes the desired hierarchy gp,n≪gχg_{p,n}\ll g_{\chi}. However, the scattering amplitude for direct detection is proportional to their product

ℳp​χ→p​χ∝gp,n​gχ≲g12,\mathcal{M}_{p\chi\to p\chi}\propto g_{p,n}g_{\chi}\lesssim g_{1}^{2}, (118)

where g1g_{1} is subject to the bounds in Fig. 4 because of the presence of the AhA_{h}, with mAh∼mAℓm_{A_{h}}\sim m_{A_{\ell}}. In other words, the effective suppression factor is again the same as what we have found before.

As a last resort, one may attempt to fine tune the vacuum expectation values such that δ​m2∼m22−m12\delta m^{2}\sim m_{2}^{2}-m_{1}^{2} even though δ​m≪m2,m1\delta m\ll m_{2},m_{1}. It is now convenient to introduce the notation

m¯2≡12​(m12+m22)\displaystyle\bar{m}^{2}\equiv\frac{1}{2}(m_{1}^{2}+m^{2}_{2}) (119)
Δ​m2≡12​(m12−m22).\displaystyle\Delta m^{2}\equiv\frac{1}{2}(m_{1}^{2}-m^{2}_{2}). (120)

The physical masses are now

mAℓ2\displaystyle m^{2}_{A_{\ell}} =m¯2​(1−δ​m4+Δ​m4/m¯2)\displaystyle=\bar{m}^{2}(1-\sqrt{\delta m^{4}+\Delta m^{4}}/\bar{m}^{2}) (121)
mAh2\displaystyle m^{2}_{A_{h}} =m¯2​(1+δ​m4+Δ​m4/m¯2).\displaystyle=\bar{m}^{2}(1+\sqrt{\delta m^{4}+\Delta m^{4}}/\bar{m}^{2}). (122)

The couplings are of the form

ℒ⊃\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\supset Aℓμ​(cos⁡θ​g1​JS​M,μ+sin⁡θ​g2​Jχ,μ)\displaystyle A_{\ell}^{\mu}\left(\cos\theta g_{1}J_{SM,\mu}+\sin\theta g_{2}J_{\chi,\mu}\right)
+Ahμ​(−sin⁡θ​g1​JS​M,μ+cos⁡θ​g2​Jχ,μ),\displaystyle+A_{h}^{\mu}\left(-\sin\theta g_{1}J_{SM,\mu}+\cos\theta g_{2}J_{\chi,\mu}\right), (123)

with θ\theta the mixing angle, as determined by the values of δ​m\delta m and Δ​m\Delta m. One can take it to be 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) by tuning δ​m≈Δ​m\delta m\approx\Delta m. From (123), we now see that AℓμA_{\ell}^{\mu} and AhμA_{h}^{\mu} will destructively interfere, with the cancellation being exact in the limit where mAℓ≈mAhm_{A_{\ell}}\approx m_{A_{h}}. At the level of the amplitude, if we expand in Δ​m,δ​m≪m¯\Delta m,\delta m\ll\bar{m}, this cancellation is only lifted by corrections that are suppressed by ∼δ​m4+Δ​m4/m¯2≪1\sim\sqrt{\delta m^{4}+\Delta m^{4}}/\bar{m}^{2}\ll 1, thus recovering the same suppression factor we found before.

In summary, we find it very difficult to build a model of a heavy axial vector mediator which can accommodate a parametrically larger direct detection rate than what we presented in Section IV. We currently are not aware of a mechanism which circumvents the argument laid out in this section.

D.3 A light mediator model

For completeness, we comment briefly on the light mediator regime of the U​(1)′×U​(1)′U(1)^{\prime}\times U(1)^{\prime} model (mAh,mAℓ≪qm_{A_{h}},m_{A_{\ell}}\ll q). In this case, we can couple the A1′A_{1}^{\prime} and A2′A_{2}^{\prime} through kinetic mixing. After diagonalizing to the mass basis and taking the non-relativistic limit, we find the effective Hamiltonian

ℋA1′⊗A2′light=4​gp​gχ​ϵ​[(𝐪⋅𝐉χ)​(𝐪⋅𝐒p)|𝐪|4−𝐉χ⋅𝐒p|𝐪|2]​ei​𝐪⋅𝐫,\mathcal{H}^{\rm light}_{A_{1}^{\prime}\otimes A_{2}^{\prime}}=4g_{p}g_{\chi}\epsilon\left[\frac{(\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{J}_{\chi})(\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{p})}{|\mathbf{q}|^{4}}-\frac{\mathbf{J}_{\chi}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{p}}{|\mathbf{q}|^{2}}\right]e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}}, (124)

with

gp≈0.22​g1andgχ=12​g2g_{p}\approx 0.22g_{1}\quad\mathrm{and}\quad g_{\chi}=\frac{1}{2}g_{2} (125)

after matching the quark current to the proton (see Section IV). The scattering rate is then given by

RA1′⊗A2′light≃σ¯A1′⊗A2′light∑dmd​ρχmχ​π3​q04v04​μp​χ6​(Jχ+1)​Jχ∫d3​v​f​(𝐯)​∫d3​q(2​π)3​|F⁡(𝐪)|2​S​(𝐪,ω),R^{\rm light}_{A_{1}^{\prime}\otimes A_{2}^{\prime}}\simeq\frac{\bar{\sigma}^{\rm light}_{A_{1}^{\prime}\otimes A_{2}^{\prime}}}{\sum_{d}m_{d}}\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{\pi}{3}\frac{q_{0}^{4}}{v_{0}^{4}\mu_{p\chi}^{6}}(J_{\chi}+1)J_{\chi}\\ \int d^{3}v\,f(\mathbf{v})\int\frac{d^{3}q}{(2\pi)^{3}}|F(\mathbf{q})|^{2}S(\mathbf{q},\omega), (126)

with the reference cross section

σ¯A1′⊗A2′light≃64​gp2​g22​ϵ2​v04​μχ63​π​q08.\bar{\sigma}^{\rm light}_{A_{1}^{\prime}\otimes A_{2}^{\prime}}\simeq\frac{64g_{p}^{2}g_{2}^{2}\epsilon^{2}v_{0}^{4}\mu_{\chi}^{6}}{3\pi q_{0}^{8}}. (127)

This model realizes the desired gp≪gχg_{p}\ll g_{\chi} hierarchy and is therefore appears promising. However, we assumed mAh,mAℓ≪q∼v0​mχm_{A_{h}},m_{A_{\ell}}\ll q\sim v_{0}m_{\chi} to derive (124), which implies extremely strong bounds on gpg_{p} (see Fig. 4). When accounting for these existing bounds, we find no open parameter space for direct detection, even when setting gχ=1g_{\chi}=1.

Appendix E Implementation in DarkELF

We have implemented in DarkELF the ability to calculate rates for four different spin dependent models. The rates used for the models are slightly modified versions from those given in the bulk of the paper, so that an energy threshold can be applied. Specifically, introducing a factor of ∫d​ω​δ​(ω−𝐪⋅𝐯+q2/(2​mχ))\int d\omega\delta(\omega-{\bf q}\cdot{\bf v}+q^{2}/(2m_{\chi})) and performing the integral over velocity vv first gives:

Rϕ\displaystyle R_{\phi} =σ¯ϕ∑dmd​ρχmχ​13​mp2v02​μχ​p4​∫ωt​hω+d​ω​∫q−q+d​q2​π\displaystyle=\frac{\bar{\sigma}_{\phi}}{\sum_{d}m_{d}}\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{1}{3}\frac{m_{p}^{2}}{v_{0}^{2}\mu_{\chi p}^{4}}\int\limits_{\omega_{th}}^{\omega_{+}}\!\!d\omega\int\limits_{q_{-}}^{q_{+}}\!\!\frac{dq}{2\pi}\,
×|Fϕ​(q)|2​|q|3mp2​S​(q,ω)​η​(vm​i​n​(q,ω))\displaystyle\hskip 2.84526pt\times|F_{\phi}(q)|^{2}\frac{|q|^{3}}{m_{p}^{2}}S(q,\omega)\,\eta(v_{min}(q,\omega)) (128)
Ra\displaystyle R_{a} =σ¯a∑dmd​ρχmχ​18​mp2​mχ2v04​μp​χ6​∫ωt​hω+d​ω​∫q−q+d​q2​π\displaystyle=\frac{\bar{\sigma}_{a}}{\sum_{d}m_{d}}\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{1}{8}\frac{m_{p}^{2}m_{\chi}^{2}}{v_{0}^{4}\mu_{p\chi}^{6}}\int\limits_{\omega_{th}}^{\omega_{+}}\!\!d\omega\int\limits_{q_{-}}^{q_{+}}\!\!\frac{dq}{2\pi}\,
×|Fa​(q)|2​|q|5mp2​mχ2​S​(q,ω)​η​(vm​i​n​(q,ω))\displaystyle\hskip 2.84526pt\times|F_{a}(q)|^{2}\frac{|q|^{5}}{m_{p}^{2}m_{\chi}^{2}}S(q,\omega)\,\eta(v_{min}(q,\omega)) (129)
RA′heavy\displaystyle R_{A^{\prime}}^{\rm heavy} =σ¯A′heavy∑dmd​ρχmχ​23​1μp​χ2​∫ωt​hω+d​ω​∫q−q+d​q2​π\displaystyle=\frac{\bar{\sigma}_{A^{\prime}}^{\rm heavy}}{\sum_{d}m_{d}}\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{2}{3}\frac{1}{\mu_{p\chi}^{2}}\int\limits_{\omega_{th}}^{\omega_{+}}\!\!d\omega\int\limits_{q_{-}}^{q_{+}}\!\!\frac{dq}{2\pi}\,
×|FA′​(q)|2​|q|​S​(q,ω)​η​(vm​i​n​(q,ω))\displaystyle\hskip 2.84526pt\times|F_{A^{\prime}}(q)|^{2}|q|S(q,\omega)\,\eta(v_{min}(q,\omega)) (130)
RA1′⊗A2′light\displaystyle R^{\rm light}_{A_{1}^{\prime}\otimes A_{2}^{\prime}} ≃σ¯A1′⊗A2′light∑dmd​ρχmχ​18​q04v04​μp​χ6​∫ωt​hω+d​ω​∫q−q+d​q2​π\displaystyle\simeq\frac{\bar{\sigma}^{\rm light}_{A_{1}^{\prime}\otimes A_{2}^{\prime}}}{\sum_{d}m_{d}}\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{1}{8}\frac{q_{0}^{4}}{v_{0}^{4}\mu_{p\chi}^{6}}\int\limits_{\omega_{th}}^{\omega_{+}}\!\!d\omega\int\limits_{q_{-}}^{q_{+}}\!\!\frac{dq}{2\pi}\,
×|FA′​(q)|2​|q|​S​(q,ω)​η​(vm​i​n​(q,ω)),\displaystyle\hskip 2.84526pt\times|F_{A^{\prime}}(q)|^{2}|q|S(q,\omega)\,\eta(v_{min}(q,\omega)), (131)

where the integration limits are

q±\displaystyle q_{\pm} ≡mχ​vm​a​x​(1±1−2​ωt​hmχ​vm​a​x2)\displaystyle\equiv m_{\chi}v_{max}\left(1\pm\sqrt{1-\frac{2\omega_{th}}{m_{\chi}v_{max}^{2}}}\,\right) (132)

and vm​a​x=ve​s​c+vev_{max}=v_{esc}+v_{e} which is the maximum DM speed in the lab frame. η\eta is defined in terms of the DM velocity distribution as:

η⁡(vm​i​n)=∫d3​v​f⁡(v)v​Θ​(v−vm​i​n),\eta(v_{min})=\int d^{3}v\frac{f(v)}{v}\Theta(v-v_{min}), (134)

limq,ω→∞Cℓ,d\displaystyle\lim_{q,\omega\to\infty}C_{\ell,d} =2​π​δ​(ω−q22​md)\displaystyle=2\pi\,\delta\left(\omega-\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{d}}\right) (135)

where Nu​c=1/∑dmdN_{uc}=1/\sum_{d}m_{d} is the number of unit cells per unit target mass and q=2​md​ωq=\sqrt{2m_{d}\omega}. In order to only plot the nuclear recoil limit for the spin dependent case, one can change the flag nuclear_recoil to True in either sigma_multiphonons_SD() or R_multiphonons_SD(). ×∑dmd∑d′md′​⟨Sp⟩2​(Jd+1)3​Jd​|FA′​(q)|2​η​(vm​i​n),\displaystyle\hskip-42.67912pt\times\sum_{d}\frac{m_{d}}{\sum_{d^{\prime}}m_{d^{\prime}}}\,\frac{\langle S_{p}\rangle^{2}(J_{d}+1)}{3J_{d}}\,|F_{A^{\prime}}(q)|^{2}\,\eta(v_{min}), (141)

as in [87].

By default, the code will return the scattering rate for the A′A^{\prime} mediator. In order to change this, use update_params(SD_op = new_op) where new_op can be selected from the list { "A’", "phi", "a", "double A’"}. The other parameter that can be changed via update_params() is the value of the ratio between gpg_{p} and gng_{n}. By default, the cross sections σ¯\bar{\sigma} refer to spin-dependent scattering off protons while the ratio gn/gpg_{n}/g_{p} is incorporated into the factor λd\lambda_{d} as defined in (54). For ϕ\phi and aa, this ratio is fixed to be the value predicted for the UV completion described in the paper. For A′A^{\prime}, we set gn/gpg_{n}/g_{p} = 1. These values can be changed via the keyword argument: update_params(gp_gn_ratio_val = new_val, set_gp_gn_ratio_val = True). To evaluate cross sections in terms of scattering on neutrons instead, one can also change the keyword argument gp_gn_ratio from "g_n/g_p" to be "g_p/g_n" and specify a ratio for gp/gng_{p}/g_{n}. All public functions are summarized in Table 5.

The spin dependent code requires several specific parameters in the yaml file for each material. This has so far been implemented for GaAs and Al2O3, but the user can add additional materials as follows: The unitcell dictionary contains all necessary parameters in a convenient form. The dictionary should have an entry for each atom in the unit cell which will form its own dictionary, containing the atomic number, multiplicity in the unit cell and information about the atom’s isotopes. For example, the ‘Ga’ dictionary takes the form:

"Ga":{"A":69, "mult":1, "isotopes":[{"A":69.,
        "frac":0.601, "atomic_spin":1.5,
        "f_p":0.0750967, "f_n":0.0}, {"A":71.,
        "frac":0.399, "atomic_spin":1.5,
        "f_p":0.154422, "f_n":0.0}]}

All isotopes should be included such that the isotope fractions add up to 1. These fractions can either be the natural abundances or the specific abundances of the particular material of interest. fpf_{p} and fnf_{n} can be obtained via the Odd-Group Model or shell model calculations, as preferred (see Table 2).
